deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. It continues a set of history lecture notes, apparently in the style of A. H. L. Heeren's Göttingen lectures on ancient states and trade, about the Phoenicians. The previous page covers Phoenicia in general and the early history of Sidon. This page has four parts. (1) The end of the history of Sidon: it was eclipsed by Tyre and was famous for its two 'sons' Agenor and Phoenix, said to have founded Tyre. It ended under alternating Babylonian and Persian rule. (2) 'Geschichte von Tyrus': Hiram, friend and ally of David and Solomon, whose alliance with Solomon opened navigation on the Arabian Gulf (Red Sea). Hiram is said to have died in 990. Under Pygmalion, described as a greedy and cruel ruler with a large faction against him, Carthage was founded, c. 880. During Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Tyre the king was Ethbaal II. New Tyre seems nevertheless to have acknowledged Babylonian sovereignty. (3) A new heading, 'Verbreitung der Phönizier durch Kolonien', with subsection 1, 'Allgemeine Ideen über die Anlagen von Pflanzstädten'. (4) A first sentence, continued on the next page, saying colonies were a necessity for every seafaring or trading people. The hand looks like a student's notebook rather than Gauss's own scientific hand, though attribution should be checked. There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical content, so there are no mathematical errors.

Historical dates follow late-18th/early-19th-century chronology and differ from modern dating. Hiram I is now dated c. 980–947 BC (or similar), not died 990. Carthage is traditionally founded 814 BC, not c. 880. These reflect the source chronology, not slips by the writer.
The king during Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Tyre (c. 586–573 BC) is now usually called Ithobaal III. 'Ethbaal II' matches older numbering.
Agenor and Phoenix as founders of Tyre are mythological figures, recorded here as the lecture presented them.

Last line: '[für] jede[?] Staaten[?] der[?] Welt[?] bedürfnisst[?]' is more plausibly 'für jedes seefahrende Volk Bedürfniß' or similar ('colonies were a need for every seafaring people'). This reading is tentative.
